title: A Warm and Koji Thanksgiving: Give Your Stuffing the Koji Butter Treatment
contentHtml:
Browned mushrooms, miso, and a splash of sake give classic sage stuffing a savory backbone, right down to the last buttery bread cube.

After making koji butter the other day, I felt like I’d just gotten a new nail gun and simply couldn’t find enough things to nail. I made compound koji butter and served it with prime rib. I made an herb koji butter to melt into the sauce for pan-roasted chicken. I added koji butter to my mashed potatoes. And finally, I turned my eyes towards the cornerstone of my Thanksgiving table: the stuffing.

My first crack at koji butter stuffing was about as straightforward as a recipe test gets. I made my tried-and true sage and sausage stuffing exactly as written, swapping the regular butter for koji butter. You start by sautéing sage sausage in butter before softening onions, celery, and herbs. Finally you finish it off with stock and eggs before folding in dried bread cubes and baking the whole thing.

I figured that if I could smell that blue cheese-like aroma in the butter alone, I ought to be able to taste some of its sweet, savory flavor in the finished stuffing. I could, but just barely. Mostly what I tasted was sage sausage.

For the next batch, I kept the sage and swapped the sausage for mushrooms. The idea was to give the stuffing some of the same savory depth the sausage brings while leaving a little more room for the flavor of the butter to come through. That got me closer, though the koji was still pretty faint. What finally did the trick was tripling down on koji. Along with the butter, I added a couple tablespoons of white miso toward the end of sautéing the vegetables, then deglazed the pot with a cup of sake. Both get their flavor in part from koji, and together they brought that sweet-savory quality I liked so much in the butter through to the finished stuffing.

As for the bread, an ordinary loaf of something soft and white is still my first choice. I’ve made stuffing with heartier sourdough or rustic loaves, but I personally love the way regular white bread gets a moist, custardy, almost bread pudding–like texture as it bakes with broth and eggs.

Every recipe I publish here is personally tested, tasted, and approved.

What I love about this recipe:

  • Koji butter brings umami depth to classic stuffing.

  • Mushrooms enhance the flavor of the koji butter without competing.

  • Miso paste and sake reinforce the sweet-savory flavor profile.

Yield: 10 to 14 servings
Active Time: About 35 minutes
Total Time: About 2 hours 15 minutes, plus time to make the koji butter

Notes:

  • Use the koji butter from the companion recipe.

  • I like using a mix of flavorful mushrooms like oyster, Maitake, or shiitake, though regular cremini or button mushrooms will work as well.

  • Use vegetable stock for a vegetarian stuffing.

  • If you’re making a half batch, use 2 eggs and bake it in a 10-inch skillet.

Ingredients

  • 2 ½ pounds (1.13 kg) white sandwich bread or soft Italian or French bread, cut into ¾-inch cubes (about 5 quarts)

  • 2 tablespoons (30 g) neutral cooking oil, such as canola or vegetable

  • 1 pound (450 g) mushrooms, tough stems removed, chopped into ¼- to ½-inch pieces

  • 8 tablespoons (115 g) koji butter, plus more for the baking dish

  • 1 large onion (about 12 ounces or 340 g), finely chopped

  • 4 large ribs celery (about 12 ounces or 340 g), finely chopped

  • 2 medium cloves garlic, minced or finely grated

  • ¼ cup minced fresh sage leaves, or 2 teaspoons dried sage

  • 2 tablespoons (about 35 g) white miso paste

  • 1 cup (240 ml) sake

  • 1 quart (950 ml) low-sodium vegetable, chicken, or turkey stock, divided

  • Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper

  • 3 large eggs

  • ¼ cup minced fresh parsley leaves, divided

Method

  1. Dry the bread. Adjust oven racks to the upper-middle and lower-middle positions and heat the oven to 275°F (135°C). Divide the bread between two rimmed baking sheets. Bake, stirring the cubes occasionally and switching the sheets from top to bottom halfway through, until a cube snapped in half is dry at its center, 45 to 50 minutes. Let cool. Increase the oven temperature to 350°F (175°C) and butter a deep 9x13-inch baking dish.

  2. Brown the mushrooms. Meanwhile, heat the oil in a large Dutch oven over medium-high heat util shimmering. Add the mushrooms, season lightly with salt, and cook, stirring occasionally, until they’ve released their liquid, the liquid has evaporated, and the mushrooms are sizzling in the butter and browned in spots, 8 to 10 minutes.

  3. Cook the aromatics and deglaze. Add the koji butter, onion, celery, garlic, and sage. Cook, stirring frequently, until the onion and celery are tender but not browned, about 5 minutes. Stir in the miso paste and let it coat the vegetables. Pour in the sake and simmer until the liquid has almost completely reduced, 4 to 6 minutes. Remove from the heat and stir in 2 cups of the stock. Taste and adjust the seasoning with salt and pepper.

  4. Mix the stuffing. Whisk the remaining 2 cups stock with the eggs and 3 tablespoons of the parsley. Slowly pour the egg mixture into the mushroom mixture, stirring constantly. Add the dried bread and fold gently, reaching down to the bottom of the pot, until the cubes are evenly moistened. Transfer to the prepared baking dish, leaving the surface a little uneven for extra crisp edges.

  5. Bake. Cover tightly with foil and bake for 45 minutes. Remove the foil and continue baking until the top is deeply golden and crisp and the center is set, 15 to 20 minutes longer. Let rest for 5 minutes, scatter the remaining tablespoon of parsley over the top, and serve.
